title: Screening paper 2
intro: Same shape as Screening paper 1, but now a wrong answer costs you marks. This paper trains you to skip: leaving a few questions blank is part of a good score.

stimuli.title: Sahyadri Castings Pvt Ltd: balances on 31 March 2026
rows: Term loan, repayable in one sum in 2029

questions.stem: Choose the words that fill both blanks: “The number of open review points ___ fallen since Monday, but a number of them ___ still waiting for the client.”

options.text: has … are
have … is
have … are
has … is

questions.reason: ‘The number of’ is one figure, so it takes a singular verb: ‘has’. ‘A number of’ means ‘several’, so it takes a plural verb: ‘are’. The plural ‘points’ pulls hurried readers to ‘have’, and the ‘a’ in ‘a number’ to ‘is’.

questions.stem: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to ‘deficit’ as it is used here: “The Indore branch closed the quarter with a deficit of ₹3 lakh.”

options.text: Shortfall
Loss
Surplus
Budget

questions.reason: A deficit is the amount by which money falls short; a surplus is the amount left over. ‘Shortfall’ and ‘loss’ mean nearly the same as ‘deficit’, and a budget is a plan, not an opposite.

questions.stem: Choose the word that fills the blank: “As the senior on the job, Tejal is responsible ___ reviewing every working paper before it reaches the manager.”

options.text: to
for
of
with

questions.reason: You are responsible for a task (‘responsible for reviewing’) and responsible to a person (‘responsible to the manager’). Before an -ing word, only ‘for’ works.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence has an error? “The office equipment / at both the Surat and Vadodara branches / were bought in 2019, / so the insurer wants a fresh valuation.”

options.text: The office equipment
at both the Surat and Vadodara branches
were bought in 2019
so the insurer wants a fresh valuation

questions.reason: ‘Equipment’ is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: ‘was bought’. The plural ‘branches’ sits between the subject and the verb and pulls hurried readers to ‘were’.

questions.stem: Choose the word or words that fill the blank: “The new expense claim form is ___ to fill in than the old one.”

options.text: more easier
easier
most easy
easiest

questions.reason: Comparing two forms needs the comparative, and ‘easy’ makes it with -er: ‘easier’. ‘More easier’ marks the comparison twice; ‘easiest’ and ‘most easy’ are superlatives, for three or more.

questions.stem:
Choose the most logical order of these sentences.
P. However, the client had not labelled about a third of the racks.
Q. This delay pushed the cut-off testing into the following week.
R. Our team planned to finish the stock count at the client’s warehouse in one day.
S. As a result, the count ran into a second day.

options.text: R, S, P, Q
R, P, Q, S
P, R, S, Q
R, P, S, Q

questions.reason: R sets out the plan; ‘However’ (P) brings the problem; ‘As a result’ (S) gives its effect; and ‘This delay’ (Q) can only come after S has described the delay. Read the linking words first and the order falls out.

questions.stem: Two days later, you report what Wasim said to the client: “I can collect the signed confirmations today.” Which version is correct?

options.text: Wasim told the client that he could collect the signed confirmations that day.
Wasim told the client that he can collect the signed confirmations today.
Wasim told the client that he could collect the signed confirmations the next day.
Wasim told the client that he could have collected the signed confirmations that day.

questions.reason: After the past ‘told’, ‘can’ moves back to ‘could’, and ‘today’ becomes ‘that day’ because you are reporting it later. ‘The next day’ changes when he meant to collect them, and ‘could have collected’ suggests he didn’t.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling for the blank: “Please send the ageing of trade ___ by Friday.”

options.text: recievables
receiveables
receivibles
receivables

questions.reason: After c, the spelling is ‘ei’: ‘receive’. Adding ‘-able’ drops the final e: ‘receivable’, ‘receivables’.

questions.stem: Read: “At Sorath Warehousing, only staff with an authorised card can open the store-room door, and the door locks itself when it closes. During busy shifts, though, staff often prop it open.” What does this tell you about the control?

options.text: It is badly designed and needs a better lock.
It is well designed but is not applied every time.
It works well, since only authorised staff have cards.
Staff are lending their cards to outsiders.

questions.reason: The card and the self-locking door are sound: that is the control’s design. Propping the door open means it isn’t applied consistently: that is how it operates. Nothing says the lock is poor or that cards are lent out.

questions.stem: Choose the most concise sentence that keeps the meaning.

options.text: In spite of the fact that the client was late with the data, we filed the return on time.
Even though the client was late with the data, even so we filed the return on time.
Although the client sent the data late, we filed the return on time.
The return was filed on time by us, in spite of the data being late from the client.

questions.reason: ‘Although’ does the work of ‘in spite of the fact that’ in one word, and the active ‘we filed’ is shorter than ‘was filed by us’. ‘Even though … even so’ says the contrast twice.

questions.stem: Corvex Logistics’ expenses for the year are 72% of its revenue, and its profit is ₹21 lakh. What is its revenue?

options.text: ₹29.2 lakh
₹54 lakh
₹75 lakh
₹96 lakh

questions.reason: Profit is the 28% of revenue left after expenses, so divide the profit by 28%. ₹29.2 lakh divides by 72%, ₹54 lakh is the expenses, and ₹96 lakh adds the profit to the revenue.
questions.working: Profit = 100% − 72% = 28% of revenue. Revenue = 21 ÷ 0.28 = ₹75 lakh. Check: expenses = 72% of 75 = ₹54 lakh, and 75 − 54 = 21.

questions.stem: In a firm, the ratio of audit staff to tax staff is 5 : 6, and the ratio of tax staff to advisory staff is 9 : 10. What is the ratio of audit staff to advisory staff?
questions.reason: Two ratios join only once their shared term, the tax staff, is made equal. 1 : 2 pairs the 5 with the 10 directly, 5 : 9 pairs the two first terms, and 25 : 27 multiplies the terms crosswise.
questions.working: 5 : 6 = 15 : 18 and 9 : 10 = 18 : 20, so audit : tax : advisory = 15 : 18 : 20. Audit : advisory = 15 : 20 = 3 : 4.

questions.stem: The chart shows a firm’s fee income in each quarter of 2025–26. Between which two quarters in a row did fee income rise by the largest percentage, and by how much?

options.text: Apr–Jun to Jul–Sep, 12.5%
Oct–Dec to Jan–Mar, 33.3%
Jul–Sep to Jan–Mar, 20%
Oct–Dec to Jan–Mar, 50%

questions.reason: Work each rise on the earlier quarter’s figure. 33.3% divides the ₹18 lakh rise by the later figure, 54; Jul–Sep to Jan–Mar skips a quarter, so the two are not in a row.
questions.working: Apr–Jun to Jul–Sep: (45 − 40) ÷ 40 = 12.5%. Jul–Sep to Oct–Dec: a fall (45 to 36). Oct–Dec to Jan–Mar: (54 − 36) ÷ 36 = 18 ÷ 36 = 50%, the largest.

questions.stem: A dealer buys office chairs at ₹2,400 each. He wants a profit of 25% on cost after giving a discount of 20% on the marked price. What marked price should he put on each chair?
questions.reason: The discount comes off the marked price, so the selling price is 80% of it: divide by 0.80. Adding 20% to the selling price gives ₹3,600, adding 25% and 20% to the cost gives ₹3,480, and ₹3,000 is the selling price itself.
questions.working: Selling price = 2,400 × 1.25 = ₹3,000. Selling price = 80% of the marked price, so marked price = 3,000 ÷ 0.80 = ₹3,750. Check: 3,750 − 20% = 3,000.

questions.stem: Gurpreet puts ₹60,000 into a scheme that pays simple interest. Four years later the balance is ₹84,000. At the same rate, how many years after the deposit will the balance reach ₹1,26,000?

options.text: 6 years
7 years
11 years
21 years

questions.reason: Simple interest adds the same ₹6,000 every year, and ₹1,26,000 needs ₹66,000 of interest. 7 years is only the time after year 4, 21 years treats the whole ₹1,26,000 as interest, and 6 years scales 4 by 1,26,000 ÷ 84,000.
questions.working: Interest in 4 years = 84,000 − 60,000 = ₹24,000, so ₹6,000 a year. Interest needed = 1,26,000 − 60,000 = ₹66,000. 66,000 ÷ 6,000 = 11 years after the deposit.

questions.stem: Working by herself, Nandini needs 24 hours to verify a client’s fixed asset register. After her first 6 hours, Manav joins in, and the two of them complete what is left in 12 hours. How many hours would Manav need on his own for the whole register?

options.text: 16 hours
24 hours
36 hours
48 hours

questions.reason: Nandini keeps working in the last 12 hours, so take her rate out of the joint rate. 16 hours gives that last part to Manav alone, 24 hours treats the 12 joint hours as the whole job, and 36 hours adds 24 and 12.
questions.working: In 6 hours Nandini does 6/24 = 1/4, so 3/4 is left. Together they do 3/4 in 12 hours: 1/16 of the job an hour. Manav’s rate = 1/16 − 1/24 = 3/48 − 2/48 = 1/48 an hour, so he needs 48 hours.

questions.stem: A train 210 m long runs at 54 km/h. How long does it take to pass completely through a platform 330 m long?

options.text: 36 seconds
22 seconds
14 seconds
10 seconds

questions.reason: The train has passed the platform only when its last coach leaves it, so it covers both lengths. 22 seconds counts the platform alone, 14 seconds the train alone, and 10 seconds divides by 54 without turning km/h into m/s.

questions.stem: A 50-litre vat at a juice unit is full of pure fruit concentrate. A worker draws out 10 litres and tops the vat up with water, then does the same once more. What percentage of the vat is now concentrate?
questions.reason: The second 10 litres drawn out is already part water, so less concentrate leaves the second time. 60% takes out 20 litres of pure concentrate, 80% stops after one round, and 36% is the water.
questions.working: Each round keeps 40/50 = 4/5 of the concentrate. After two rounds: 50 × 4/5 × 4/5 = 32 litres. 32 ÷ 50 = 64%.

questions.stem: A senior must pick 4 of the 9 articles in her team for a stock count. How many different groups of 4 can she pick?
questions.reason: A group ignores order, so divide the 3,024 ordered picks by the 24 orders of each group of 4. 36 is 9 × 4, and 6,561 lets the same article be picked more than once.
questions.working: Ordered picks = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3,024. Orders of 4 people = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. Groups = 3,024 ÷ 24 = 126.

questions.stem: A discount of 32% on an order would save ₹27,000 more than a discount of 20%. What is the value of the order?
questions.reason: The ₹27,000 is the gap between the two discounts: 12% of the order. ₹84,375 and ₹1,35,000 treat it as the whole 32% or the whole 20%, and ₹3,24,000 multiplies by 12 instead of dividing by 12%.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series? CX, EW, GV, IU, ?

options.text: JT
KU
LT
KT

questions.reason: Track each letter on its own: the first moves two places forward, the second one place back. JT moves the first letter only one place, KU forgets to move the second, and LT moves the first three places.
questions.working: First letters: C, E, G, I, K (+2 each time). Second letters: X, W, V, U, T (−1 each time). Next: KT.

questions.stem: Six partners sit around a round table, facing the centre. Two seatings count as the same only when everyone has the same neighbour on the left and the same neighbour on the right. How many different seatings are there?
questions.reason: Moving everyone one seat round keeps every neighbour, so it is the same seating: a circle of 6 has (6 − 1)! = 120, not 6! = 720. 60 halves 120, which is right only when a seating and its mirror image count as one; 360 halves 720.
questions.working: Fix one partner’s seat; the other 5 can sit in 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120 orders.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some analysts are cyclists. Every cyclist is an early riser.
Conclusion: Some early risers are analysts.
If both statements are true, what can you say about the conclusion?

options.text: It must be true
It must be false
It may or may not be true

questions.reason: The analysts who cycle are early risers, so at least those early risers are analysts. The conclusion reverses the order of the words, but ‘some’ works both ways, so it must be true.

questions.stem: A client’s list of debtors is sorted by the amount each one owes. Girnar Traders comes 17th counting from the top and 31st counting from the bottom. How many debtors are on the list?
questions.reason: Each count includes Girnar Traders, so adding the two counts it twice: take one off. 48 counts it twice, and 46 leaves it out altogether.

questions.stem: Standing at the office gate facing south, Zoya turns 45° to her left, then 180° to her right, then 90° to her left. Which way is she facing now?

options.text: North-east
North-west
South-east
South-west

questions.reason: Add the turns first, then apply them once: a net 45° to the right of south is south-west. South-east turns the wrong way, north-west stops before the last turn, and north-east leaves out the 180° turn.
questions.working: Count right turns as plus and left turns as minus: −45 + 180 − 90 = +45. Turning right from south swings towards west, so 45° on from south is south-west.

questions.stem: Rewa is Mohan’s daughter. Mohan is also the father of Keshav, and Keshav is Parth’s father. How is Rewa related to Parth?

options.text: Cousin
Paternal aunt
Maternal aunt
Grandmother

questions.reason: Rewa and Keshav are both Mohan’s children, so Rewa is Keshav’s sister, and Keshav is Parth’s father. A father’s sister is a paternal aunt; ‘maternal’ would need the link to run through Parth’s mother, and a cousin would be Rewa’s child, in Parth’s own generation.

questions.stem: Six boxes of a client’s files sit on a rack of six shelves, one box to a shelf, shelf 1 at the top. Payroll is directly below TDS. Sales is somewhere above TDS. Bank is somewhere above Sales. Cash is somewhere below Bank. GST is on neither the top shelf nor the bottom shelf. Which of these must be true?

options.text: GST is directly above Sales
Payroll is on the bottom shelf
Bank is on the top shelf
Sales is on shelf 2

questions.reason: Bank is above Sales, TDS and Payroll, and above Cash, so only GST could sit above Bank, and GST is never on shelf 1. Payroll is often at the bottom, but Cash can take the bottom shelf instead.
questions.working: Bank is above Sales, Sales above TDS, and Payroll directly below TDS; Cash is below Bank; GST is not on shelf 1. So shelf 1 is Bank. Racks that fit include Bank, Sales, TDS, Payroll, GST, Cash (Payroll not at the bottom, GST not above Sales) and Bank, GST, Cash, Sales, TDS, Payroll (Sales on shelf 4).

questions.stem: Tarangini Dairy’s staff fell from 120 to 110 this year, yet its salary cost rose by 6%. Which of these, if true, best explains both facts?

options.text: Ten employees left during the year, and the company did not replace them.
Its sales fell this year because two large customers moved to a rival.
Salaries were raised sharply this year, and last year’s arrears were paid too.
It installed new machines that need fewer people to run them.

questions.reason: Fewer people can still cost more if each is paid more, so only a sharp pay rise, with arrears on top, explains both facts. The staff leaving and the new machines explain only the smaller headcount, and sales don’t set salaries.

questions.stem:
What does one desk lamp cost?
I. Three desk lamps and two extension boards cost ₹4,100 in all.
II. A lamp costs ₹300 more than an extension board.
Which statements, if any, are enough to answer the question?

options.text: Statement I alone is enough, but II alone is not
Statement II alone is enough, but I alone is not
Each statement alone is enough
Both statements together are enough, but neither alone is
Even both statements together are not enough

questions.reason: Each statement is one equation in two unknown prices, so neither alone fixes the lamp’s price. Two different equations together fix both prices; you need not find the price to answer.
questions.working: I alone: 3 lamps + 2 boards = ₹4,100 fits lamp ₹900 with board ₹700, and lamp ₹1,100 with board ₹400. II alone: lamp = board + ₹300 fits any board price. Together: let a board cost ₹b, so a lamp costs ₹(b + 300). 3(b + 300) + 2b = 4,100, so 5b + 900 = 4,100, b = ₹640 and the lamp costs ₹940.

questions.stem: In a code, LOAN is written 5821 and GOAL is written 3825. How is LONG written in this code?
questions.reason: Both words give L = 5, O = 8 and A = 2; only LOAN gives N = 1 and only GOAL gives G = 3, so you need both. L, O, N, G is 5, 8, 1, 3; 5831 swaps N and G.

questions.stem: Which of these is capital expenditure for Trivedi Steel Tubes Ltd?

options.text: Renewing its accounting software licence for another year
Repainting the office walls as part of routine upkeep
Paying the yearly maintenance charge for its lifts
Buying and installing a new server rack for its office

questions.reason: The server rack is a new asset that will serve the business for years, so its cost, installation included, is capital. The renewal, the repainting and the maintenance only keep things running for the year: revenue.

questions.stem: On 31 March 2026, the cash book of Ambar Ceramics Pvt Ltd shows ₹2,40,000 in its current account (money in the bank, not an overdraft). A cheque of ₹35,000 that it gave a supplier on 29 March has not yet been presented to the bank. There is no other difference. What balance does the bank statement show?
questions.reason: A cheque issued lowers the cash book at once but the bank balance only when it is presented, so the bank still shows the ₹35,000. ₹2,05,000 takes the cheque off a second time.
questions.working: The cash book has already deducted ₹35,000; the bank has not. Bank statement = 2,40,000 + 35,000 = ₹2,75,000.

questions.stem: Pankhudi Couriers Pvt Ltd follows AS. Under AS 3, where in its cash flow statement does it show the cash it paid for a new delivery van?

options.text: Cash flows from investing activities
Cash flows from operating activities, since the van is used for daily deliveries
Cash flows from financing activities
Nowhere, since buying an asset does not change the profit

questions.reason: Cash paid to acquire long-term assets such as vehicles is an investing outflow. Using the van in daily work does not make its purchase operating, and financing covers loans and share capital.

questions.stem: Kumud Tiles Pvt Ltd follows AS and trades in tiles. Under AS 2, which of these costs goes into the cost of its closing stock?

options.text: Rent of the showroom where the tiles are displayed for sale
Tiles broken by careless handling, far beyond the normal level
Freight paid to bring the tiles it bought to its warehouse
Storage charges for tiles that are waiting for buyers

questions.reason: The cost of purchase includes freight inward: it brings the stock to its present location. AS 2 leaves out abnormal wastage, selling costs such as showroom rent, and storage costs unless a production process needs them.

questions.stem: A customer who owes Tamrapat Fixtures Pvt Ltd ₹48,000 has closed down, and nothing will be recovered. The company has made no provision for doubtful debts. What is the effect of writing off the debt?

options.text: Trade receivables fall by ₹48,000 and a ₹48,000 bad-debt expense cuts profit
Trade receivables fall by ₹48,000, and cash falls by the same amount
Nothing is recorded until the customer’s affairs are finally wound up
A liability of ₹48,000 is recorded in the customer’s name

questions.reason: A debt that will never be paid is no longer an asset, so receivables fall and the loss is an expense of the year. No cash moves, and waiting for the customer’s affairs to close would overstate the asset.
questions.working: Bad debts Dr ₹48,000; To the customer’s account (trade receivables) ₹48,000.

questions.stem: From the balances in the table, what is the company’s working capital?

options.text: ₹5 lakh
₹17 lakh
₹19 lakh
₹28 lakh

questions.reason: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities. The term loan falls due only in 2029, so it is not current: taking it off gives ₹5 lakh. ₹19 lakh misses the outstanding expenses, and ₹28 lakh is the current assets alone.
questions.working: Current assets = 14 + 11 + 3 = ₹28 lakh. Current liabilities = 9 + 2 = ₹11 lakh. Working capital = 28 − 11 = ₹17 lakh.

questions.stem: Vanshika Pharma Ltd works out that a new packing line has an internal rate of return (IRR) of 14%. What does this tell you?

options.text: The line’s cash inflows, simply added up, come to 14% more than its cost.
The company’s cost of capital must also be 14%.
The line will pay back its cost in about 7 years, that is, 100 ÷ 14.
Discounted at 14%, the inflows are worth exactly the cost, so NPV is zero.

questions.reason: IRR is the discount rate at which the present value of the inflows equals the outlay, so NPV is zero at that rate. Simply adding the inflows ignores the time value of money; the IRR is compared with the cost of capital, not equal to it; payback is a different measure.

questions.stem: Vouching 40 purchase invoices of Vindhya Forgings Pvt Ltd, you find 39 in order; on one, the amount looks overwritten. What does professional scepticism ask of you?

options.text: Treat every invoice in the file as forged until each supplier confirms it in writing
Accept it, since the other 39 invoices from the same file were in order
Check the overwritten one against the goods receipt and the payment
Report the purchase manager to the Board for forgery at once

questions.reason: Scepticism is a questioning mind, not doubt of everything: records can be taken as genuine unless something gives you reason to doubt them, and the overwritten amount does. Accepting it ignores the warning sign; doubting every invoice or accusing someone goes past the evidence.

questions.stem: You are testing whether every trade payable of Pinewood Interiors LLP at 31 March 2026 has been recorded. Which procedure helps most?

options.text: Vouch a sample of the March purchase bills already in the ledger to their invoices
Recompute the totals of the payables ledger and agree them to the trial balance
Send confirmation requests to the five suppliers with the largest balances recorded in the ledger
Look through April and May payments and supplier statements for March bills never booked

questions.reason: To find what is missing, start outside the books: later payments and the suppliers’ own statements show bills that should have been recorded. Vouching, recomputing and confirming the largest balances test only what is already recorded.

questions.stem: Which Standard on Auditing sets out what the auditor must do about fraud when auditing financial statements?

options.text: SA 230
SA 240
SA 315
SA 570

questions.reason: SA 240 covers the auditor’s responsibilities relating to fraud. SA 230 is audit documentation, SA 315 identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement, and SA 570 going concern.

questions.stem: An article compares a factory’s monthly power bills with its machine hours and asks why November’s bill jumped while the machine hours stayed flat. What kind of audit procedure is this?

options.text: An analytical procedure
An external confirmation
A physical inspection
A test of the control over approvals

questions.reason: Analytical procedures study plausible relationships between financial and non-financial data, here power cost and machine hours, and follow up on figures that break the pattern (SA 520). Nothing is confirmed with an outsider or inspected.

questions.stem: Which event brings a transaction into the GST net?

options.text: The manufacture of goods in a factory
Earning income from a business
The supply of goods or services, or both
The sale of goods, but not the supply of services

questions.reason: GST is a tax on supply, and it covers services as well as goods. Manufacture is the event for central excise, which GST largely replaced, and income is taxed under income tax.

questions.stem: Rehana runs a consultancy and is not in any presumptive scheme. Her tax for tax year 2026–27 is estimated at ₹4,00,000, and advance tax applies. How much advance tax should she have paid in all by 15 December 2026?
questions.reason: By 15 December the total paid should reach 75% of the year’s tax. ₹1,80,000 is the September total (45%), ₹1,20,000 is the December instalment alone (30%), and the full ₹4,00,000 is due by 15 March.
questions.working: Cumulative: 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December, 100% by 15 March. 75% of 4,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

questions.stem: Where do you look for Quillbyte Software Pvt Ltd’s own rules for managing its internal affairs, such as how its directors are appointed and how its shares may be transferred?

options.text: Its Memorandum of Association
Its Articles of Association
Its register of members
Its latest annual return

questions.reason: The Articles hold the regulations for managing the company. The Memorandum sets out its objects and the scope of its business; the register of members and the annual return record facts, not rules.

questions.stem: Indrayani Agro Ltd follows AS. On 1 April 2025 it borrowed ₹10 crore to build a new plant that will take about two years to get ready for use. Under AS 16, how does it treat the interest for 2025–26, while the plant is being built?

options.text: As a finance cost in the profit and loss statement
As a deduction from reserves, outside the profit and loss statement
As a note to the accounts only, until the plant is in use
As part of the cost of the plant, a qualifying asset

questions.reason: An asset that takes a substantial period (ordinarily 12 months or more) to get ready for use is a qualifying asset, so interest directly attributable to it is capitalised while it is being built. Once the plant is ready, the interest is expensed.

questions.stem: Two seniors on your client each want different work first this morning: Ashwin the TDS reconciliation, Megha the fixed asset schedule. You can’t finish both by noon. What do you do?

options.text: Tell both about the clash now and ask them, or the manager, which comes first
Start with the shorter one, so that at least one piece of work is ready by noon
Work on the two by turns, so that neither senior feels left out
Do the one the more senior of the two asked for, and don’t tell the other

questions.reason: Only the seniors or the manager can set the order, and both need to know before noon; confirm what they decide in a short message. Choosing yourself, by length or by seniority, leaves one senior counting on work that won’t come, and working by turns finishes neither.

questions.stem: An email, apparently from a client’s finance head, says the file-sharing link has expired and asks you to sign in again with your firm password through a link. The sender’s address is one letter off. What do you do?

options.text: Sign in through the link quickly, since you need the ledgers today
Reply to the same email and ask the sender to confirm that it is genuine
Forward it to your teammates so that they know to be careful
Don’t click or reply; report it to IT and phone the client

questions.reason: A look-alike address asking for your password is a phishing mail. A reply goes straight back to the sender, and forwarding spreads the link; report it the way your firm asks, and check with the client on a number you already have.

questions.stem: The client’s accountant still hasn’t sent statements for three of the twelve bank accounts, despite two reminders. At 5 pm he asks you to confirm that the bank reconciliation review is ‘on track’ for Friday. What do you reply?

options.text: “Yes, it’s on track,” and sort out the three with your senior later
“Nine of twelve are done. With the other three statements by 11 am tomorrow, we can finish by Friday.”
“It’s behind because your team is slow; nothing more we can do.”
“I can’t say; please ask my senior,” and leave it there

questions.reason: Give the client the true status, what it depends on and when you need it, so he can act, and keep your senior posted. ‘On track’ to keep the peace is untrue, blame gives no next step, and passing it on answers nothing.

questions.stem: You need to group a client’s 600-line trial balance into schedules tonight. A friend says a free public AI chatbot does it in seconds. What do you do?

options.text: Use only the tools your firm has approved for client data; ask your senior if unsure
Take out the client’s name and paste the rest, so nothing identifies the client
Paste it in, since the output is only a draft that you will check line by line
Paste half the lines at a time, so the chatbot never sees the client’s whole trial balance

questions.reason: Client data stays inside the systems your firm has approved. Removing the name doesn’t make it safe: ledger names, amounts and patterns can still point to the client, and the figures are confidential anyway. Checking the output later doesn’t undo the upload.

questions.stem: At a client, payments above ₹1 lakh need two signatures. In your sample of 25, one ₹3.2 lakh payment has only one. The accounts head says, “It was a one-time rush; please keep it out of your file.” What do you do?

options.text: Get the second signature on the voucher now, then mark the item as passed
Record the exception and its cause, and take it to your senior to judge its effect
Note it as a ‘one-time rush’, as the accounts head explained, and conclude the control works
Keep it out of the file, but mention it to your senior when you next meet

questions.reason: A failed item stays in the file: you and your senior judge why it failed, whether the control can still be relied on and whether to test more. Signing it now alters the evidence, and taking ‘one-time’ on trust or keeping it off the file hides a control failure.

questions.stem: Preparing a client’s fixed asset schedule, you aren’t sure whether a major overhaul that adds five years to a machine’s life should be capitalised or expensed. It is due tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Expense it, since your Inter notes treated repairs as an expense
Use the treatment that a similar client of the firm followed for its overhaul last year
Leave it for the reviewer to catch, since time is short
Check AS 10, discuss it with your senior, and record the conclusion with its reason

questions.reason: Settle a technical doubt from the standard and with your senior, and record why, so the reviewer sees the basis. Memory and another client’s choice may not fit these facts, and leaving it for the reviewer passes on a problem you have already spotted.

questions.stem: A fellow article is stuck on a GST reconciliation and asks for your help. Your own schedule is due to your senior in two hours. What do you do?

options.text: Help her briefly on the point she is stuck on; if it needs more, tell your senior
Tell her to take it to the senior, since your schedule is due soon
Drop your own schedule and work on hers until it is done, then explain to your senior
Send her your file from another client so that she can copy its method

questions.reason: A few minutes on her sticking point helps the team and keeps your own deadline; when both can’t be done, your senior sets the order. Sending her straight to the senior refuses help you can spare, dropping your work unannounced misses your deadline, and another client’s file is confidential.

questions.stem: In review, your senior says a provision you called ‘adequate’ is ₹2 lakh short, and the client will book the extra. She adds, “No need to change your working paper; my review note covers it.” What do you do?

options.text: Leave the working paper as it is, since the review note records the change
Update the working paper to show the final conclusion and the reason, and tell her
Ask the client to countersign your old working paper to show they accepted the change
Change the amount in the working paper but leave the conclusion ‘adequate’ as it was

questions.reason: The working paper must show the final conclusion and how it was reached. Review notes are usually cleared once answered, so a file that leans on them ends up calling the provision adequate when it wasn’t; a new amount under the old conclusion contradicts itself.

questions.stem: Which body recommends accounting and auditing standards for companies, monitors compliance with them, and oversees the quality of audits of listed and other specified companies?

options.text: National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)
Reserve Bank of India (RBI)

questions.reason: NFRA, set up under the Companies Act, 2013, recommends accounting and auditing standards, monitors compliance with them and oversees audit quality for specified companies. SEBI regulates the securities market, the CAG audits government accounts, and the RBI regulates banks and money.
